text:
He didn’t do miracles?! 🤔

“Scores of Church members on both sides of the river fell ill. The residents of the temporary tent city surrounding the Prophet’s home were stricken by the disease as were the Saints staying in his home. Emma nursed the people night and day, while Joseph’s six-year-old son carried water for the sick until he also caught the disease. The pestilence was indiscriminate, affecting all ages and classes. One of the early fatalities in the city was Oliver Huntington’s mother, Zina. The Prophet Joseph invited Oliver to bring his family, who were all ill, to his home for needed care. The Whitney family was in a similar situation. Elizabeth Ann reported that they “were only just barely able to crawl around and wait upon each other.” In those circumstances Elizabeth gave birth to her ninth child. When Joseph learned of their plight he insisted that the family move in with him. They accepted his offer and took up residence in a small cottage in Joseph’s yard. By 12 July, Joseph Smith, Sr., was so ill he was near death.

Eventually Joseph Smith also became ill, but after several days’ confinement he was prompted to arise and extend help to others. The day of 22 July was, in the words of Wilford Woodruff, “a day of God’s power” in Nauvoo and Montrose. That morning the Prophet arose and, being filled with the Spirit of the Lord, administered to the sick in his house and in the yard outside. More sick people were down by the river, and there too he administered with great power to the faithful. One such, Henry G. Sherwood, was near death. Joseph stepped to the door of Brother Sherwood’s tent and commanded him to rise and come out; he obeyed and was healed. Elder Heber C. Kimball and others accompanied the Prophet across the river to Montrose. One by one they visited the homes of the Twelve and administered to those who needed a blessing. Brigham Young, Wilford Woodruff, Orson Pratt, and John Taylor then joined Joseph in his mission of mercy.

One of the most memorable of the healings in Montrose was that of Elijah Fordham. When the brethren arrived he was lying in bed unable to speak.

“Brother Joseph walked up to Brother Fordham, and took him by the right hand. …

“He saw that Brother Fordham’s eyes were glazed, and that he was speechless and unconscious.

“After taking hold of his hand, he looked down into the dying man’s face and said: ‘Brother Fordham, do you not know me?’ At first he made no reply; but we could all see the effect of the Spirit of God resting upon him.

“He again said: ‘Elijah, do you not know me?’

“With a low whisper, Brother Fordham answered, ‘Yes!’

“The Prophet then said, ‘Have you not faith to be healed?’

“The answer, which was a little plainer than before, was: ‘I am afraid it is too late. If you had come sooner, I think it might have been.’

“He had the appearance of a man waking from sleep. It was the sleep of death.

“Joseph then said: ‘Do you believe that Jesus is the Christ?’

“‘I do, Brother Joseph,’ was the response.

“Then the Prophet of God spoke with a loud voice, as in the majesty of the Godhead: ‘Elijah, I command you, in the name of Jesus of Nazareth, to arise and be made whole!’

“The words of the Prophet were not like the words of man, but like the voice of God. It seemed to me that the house shook from its foundation.

“Elijah Fordham leaped from his bed like a man raised from the dead. A healthy color came to his face, and life was manifested in every act.”

text:
An overweight Benny Lynch is knocked out in the 3rd round by Aurel Toma (left), on October 3, 1938, at Empress Hall, Earl's Court, London, UK.

This would be the final bout of Lynch's career.

The Brisbane Courier would report:

"Benny Lynch, former king of the flyweights, and at present, an 'overweight king,' suffered the greatest humiliation of his career, when he was knocked out by the Romanian bantamweight, Aurel Toma in the 3rd round at the National Sporting Club. Lynch, who weighed almost a stone heavier than his opponent, was flabby and dull-eyed, a caricature of his former greatness. He made spasmodic efforts at punching and moved sluggishly out of the range of Toma, who was trained to the minute. The Romanian punched with both hands and floored Lynch with a right to the jaw and a left to the body, lifting Lynch off his feet. This was Lynch's first knockout loss, and it was greeted with boos from the crowd of 10,000. Commentators stated that Lynch appeared to collapse because of his own weight and that Toma merely contributed."

After this bout, the National Sporting Club announced that it has offered to finance Benny Lynch an opportunity for rehabilitation. The NSC stated that, with an eye towards fighting for and winning the bantamweight championship of the world from Sixto Escobar - in order for Lynch to regain his form - he would be required to spend two weeks in a nursing home, and later in the month, to check into a country Sanitorium. After that he would be required to sign on as a deck hand on a freighter in order to toughen himself up before going into training. The NSC was providing 400 pounds Sterling, which Lynch agreed to. However, Lynch never fought again.

Benny Lynch is considered by some to be among the finest boxers below the lightweight division in his era and has been described by many as the greatest fighter Scotland has ever produced. 

The Ring Magazine founder Nat Fleischer rated Lynch as the #5 flyweight of all-time while his publication placed him 63rd in its 2002 list of the "Best Fighters of the Last 80 Years".

Benny Lynch would battle with alcoholism for the rest of his life despite several attempts to treat the disease. He died in 1946 of malnutrition-induced respiratory failure, at the far too young age of 33. 

He was buried at St. Kentigern's Cemetery, in Glasgow, with some 2,000 people attending the funeral.

Lynch's life was the subject of Bill Bryden's 1974 stage play Benny Lynch, with a book of the play published in 1975, and a television adaptation made in 1976. A second play based on Lynch's life, written by Peter Arnett, was first performed in 1985.

The Benny Lynch Story, a stage play written by David Carswell and directed by David Hayman Jr, with Stephen Purdon playing the boxing champion, toured Scotland in May and June of 2019.

Aurel Toma, born in Badabag, Romania and fighting out of Ventura, California, went 47-16-11 (15 KO's) as a pro. He never fought for a world title.

You’re right that a divided Right loses. You’re wrong if the conclusion is “everyone must simply fold into Reform.” 
That is how you get more Kent by-elections, not fewer.

Rupert Lowe already made a public offer of talks. Reform answered with preconditions, insults to the voter base, and a refusal to treat Restore as a real force rather than a nuisance. That was inflexible and unrealistic. You cannot lecture patriots about “consolidation” while dismissing the people who actually moved the Overton Window.

@RupertLowe10 and @RestoreBritain continually move the Overton Window,  the rest of the so-called “right” barely have the balls to peer through the corner.

There is no value in putting puppets who have already been in government and are directly responsible back into office, none at all.

Without a Unite the Right agreement, expect chaos in every election moving forward.

Restore has 180k+ members and is still rising. Restore Britain is now in 118 constituencies. Only 36% of that base would even consider Reform. Those votes do not transfer if Restore vanishes. The kill switch is already there, and Restore Members will use it.

• 55 candidates on 3–4% in Reform’s key seats is enough to split the vote and keep Farage out of No.10.
• 96 candidates on 7% and Reform drops behind the Tories once tactical voting starts.
• 118 constituencies are ready to stand Restore candidates, this is growing daily.

That’s a wipeout for Reform. No more “least worst.” That cycle already failed.

A serious pact is simple and fair: no three-way fights in target seats, agreed non-aggression where one party is clearly stronger, shared ground on borders and remigration, and an end to the personality war. Lowe put an offer on the table. Reform made it about conditions and control. That is why the Right is still split three ways.

The Left is consolidating. The Right is being played. Unite the Right or Restore Britain, or bust.

Grok $GTII complaint summary 

The SEC filed this complaint on October 2, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (Case No. 26 Civ. 8713): Securities and Exchange Commission v. David Reichman, et al.

Parties. The defendant is David Reichman, former CEO and Chairman of Global Tech Industries Group, Inc. (Global Tech), a Nevada corporation whose stock was quoted on OTC Link. Relief defendants are his daughter, Justine Reichman, and the Justine Reichman 2021 Trust (of which she is trustee).

Core allegations. From about 2016 through June 2024, Reichman allegedly ran a scheme in which he caused Global Tech to issue tens of millions of shares to his daughter, ex-wife, girlfriend, her son and friend, an affiliated entity (DOT8, Inc.), and others. The issuances were presented as payment for services to the company. The SEC claims Reichman knew, or recklessly disregarded, that those recipients provided no services. The result, according to the complaint, was dilution of existing shareholders.

Global Tech is described as having minimal operations, revenue, and employees during the period (essentially Reichman and a former president), large net losses, and an accumulated deficit of about $346 million by 2023. Reichman controlled the company and held majority voting rights.

Notable specifics alleged include:

More than 32 million shares issued between 2016 and 2019 to the share recipients and falsely reported in Forms 10-K as compensation for services. Justine Reichman received about 9 million shares; DOT8 received about 6 million; others received millions more.

An issuance of 940,000 shares to one individual who sold them for roughly $1.5 million and transferred about $1.4 million (90%) back to Reichman.

An August 2021 S-1 that raised about $3.3 million while omitting Justine Reichman’s beneficial ownership of nearly 16 million shares (about 6.9% of the company). Reichman allegedly directed deletions from shareholder lists and non-disclosure of related Schedule 13G filings.

Authorization of the sale of 10 million shares from an employee trust in 2022 (about $2 million proceeds, of which roughly $1.8 million went to Reichman), while filings falsely stated the shares remained uncommitted.

Failure to timely file Form 4 reports of his own stock sales.
Sales of the fraudulently issued shares generating about $8 million for Justine Reichman and about $1 million for Reichman; roughly $2.5 million of those proceeds were used to buy a home held by the 2021 trust.

The complaint also notes that a receiver removed Global Tech management in September 2024, and that a tolling agreement extends the limitations period as to Reichman to October 27, 2026.

Claims. The SEC alleges violations of Securities Act Section 17(a), Exchange Act Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 (fraud), Exchange Act Section 16(a) and Rule 16a-3 (failure to file Form 4s), and aiding and abetting Global Tech’s violations of Exchange Act Section 13(a) and Rule 13a-1 (false or misleading periodic reports). It also seeks unjust enrichment recovery from the relief defendants.

Relief sought. Permanent injunctions against further violations; a bar on Reichman participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of securities (other than for his own account); an officer-and-director bar; disgorgement with prejudgment interest (including roughly $2.5 million tied to the 2021 offering and about $1 million from stock sales as to Reichman, and about $8 million plus home-related proceeds as to the relief defendants); civil penalties; and a jury trial.

These are unproven allegations. The complaint does not reflect any adjudication or admission of liability.

text:
LET US EXTEND A HELPING HAND TO OUR TEMPLE PRIESTS 
Just pause for a minute… and open your heart.
We go to a temple.
We have Darshan of Swami.
We perform Archana.
We offer Abhishekam.
We put our offerings into the Hundi.
We pray for our family… our health… our children's future… our prosperity.
But…
Do we ever stop and think about the person who stands behind that Sanctum every single day?
The Kurukkal…
The person who wakes up before sunrise…
Who opens the temple doors…
Who cleans the Sanctum…
Who lights the lamp…
Who rings the bell…
Who chants the Mantras…
Who performs Abhishekam…
Who prepares and offers Naivedyam…
And who, with folded hands, prays for our families before Swami.
And then…
He goes back home.
Perhaps to a house with a leaking roof.
Perhaps to an empty kitchen.
Perhaps to medicines that need to be purchased.
Perhaps to a child's school fees waiting to be paid.
Perhaps to an ageing wife who needs treatment.
Perhaps to his own tired and ageing body.
Yet the next morning, he is back again.
Because there is one thought in his heart:
“Swami's Puja must never stop.”
Especially in the small, interior villages of Tamil Nadu, there are temples where only a handful of devotees visit.
There may be little income.
There may be no regular support.
There may be almost no facilities.
But…
THE PUJA CONTINUES.
The lamp continues to burn.
The bell continues to ring.
The Mantras continue to echo.
Because one Kurukkal refuses to abandon his Kainkaryam.
Sometimes, he may not even know where his next month's income will come from.
But he knows one thing:
Swami must be worshipped.
That is his dedication.
That is his Dharma.
That is his Kainkaryam.
And perhaps…
we can become the support that he desperately needs.
We can provide groceries for a month.
We can provide oil for the temple lamp and Abhishekam.
We can provide Puja materials.
We can help with medical expenses.
We can support a child's education.
We can repair a small portion of a damaged priest's house.
 We can help with an urgent family need.
It may be only a few hundred rupees for us.
But for them…
it may mean food for a family.
It may mean medicine for an elderly priest.
It may mean a child's school fee being paid.
It may mean a lamp continuing to burn.
And above all…
It may tell a Kurukkal:
“You are not alone. We are with you.”
We go to the temple to receive blessings from Swami.
They remain in the temple to serve Swami.
Let us therefore serve those who serve Him.
 The lamp they light should never go out because of poverty.
The daily Puja should never stop because the Kurukkal has no means to survive.
A family that has dedicated its life to Swami should never feel forgotten.
Remember…
Protecting a temple is not merely about protecting its walls, Gopuram or Vimanam.
A temple can have a magnificent Gopuram.
It can have a newly renovated Sanctum.
It can have beautiful stonework.
But…
Who will perform the Nitya Puja if there is no Kurukkal?
Who will light the lamp?
Who will chant the Mantras?
Who will offer Naivedyam?
Who will stand before Swami and pray for us?
That is why…

KURUKKAL FIRST… 
TEMPLE NEXT...

Let us wipe away a Kurukkal's tears.
Let us reduce a family's burden.
Let us support a child's education.
Let us help an elderly priest obtain medical treatment.
Let us put groceries into an empty kitchen.
Let us put oil into a temple lamp.
Let us ensure that the Nitya Puja continues without interruption.
This is not charity alone.
This is Kainkaryam.
This is Dharma.
This is our responsibility towards our Sanatana heritage.
We seek Swami's blessings every day.
Let us also remember the person who stands before Swami every day seeking nothing for himself, but praying for all of us.
A small contribution from us can become a great support in his life.
Let us not wait for them to ask.
Let us reach them before they are forced to give up.
Save Our Priests.
Support Our Kurukkals.
Keep the Nitya Puja Alive.
Let the Temple Lamp Continue to Burn.

text:
Mike, I appreciate you sharing this. I actually agree with Grok on one thing. There's no way for us to prove Stephanie White intentionally sabotaged the Indiana Fever.

But good grief... how many excuses are we going to make for this woman?

Read through Grok's analysis again. Every time it acknowledges something White did poorly, it immediately offers an explanation for why we shouldn't hold her responsible.

Injuries, fatigue, matchups, roster construction, defensive limitations, personnel issues, player management... you name it.

At what point do we start holding the HEAD COACH responsible for the basketball being played?

I've coached this game for 25 years, and I can tell you that some of the things we watched this season defied basic basketball logic.

Let's start with Caitlin Clark.

We have a generational point guard who is arguably the most dangerous player in basketball with the ball in her hands. She can break down defenses, create shots for herself, generate open looks for teammates, and completely change the pace of a game.

And what did we watch Stephanie White do repeatedly?

Take the ball out of her hands. Slow the game down. Run unnecessary dribble handoffs. Allow the offense to become stagnant while Kelsey Mitchell dribbled into another ridiculously difficult contested shot.

And the kicker? When Caitlin was allowed to control the offense and push the tempo, we repeatedly saw how dangerous this team could be.

So why in the hell did we keep going back to the same nonsense?

Then there's Kelsey Mitchell.

I've said all season that Kelsey might be the best player in the WNBA at turning absolutely NOTHING into points. That's an enormous compliment to her talent and an equally enormous criticism of the offense she's being asked to play in.

How many times did we watch her receive the basketball with little movement around her, the shot clock winding down, and everybody expecting her to manufacture a miracle?

That's offensive coaching, Mike.

And I haven't even gotten to the defense.

Grok acknowledges that Indiana's defense was a major problem. Well, WHO THE HELL WAS RESPONSIBLE FOR COACHING IT?

Stephanie White is the head coach, and Briann January was brought in as the defensive specialist.

Yet we spent the season watching missed rotations, poor help-side positioning, questionable switching, breakdowns on screens, and some of the worst defensive rebounding fundamentals I've seen from a professional basketball team.

We weren't talking about complicated defensive concepts either. We were watching basic mistakes that should have been addressed in practice.

And they kept happening.

Week after week. Game after game.

Now let's talk about Makayla Timpson.

How many times did we watch that young woman provide exactly what Indiana was missing? Energy, rebounding, rim protection, athleticism, and a legitimate presence around the basket.

And how many times did Stephanie White reward her by sending her right back to the bench?

We watched the same thing happen with other players. Myisha Hines-Allen gave this team valuable minutes. Lexie Hull's role became difficult to understand. Sophie Cunningham's value in creating spacing and movement was obvious.

Yet the rotations frequently looked like someone was pulling names out of a hat.

And don't even get me started on the way Caitlin's minutes were managed.

There were games where she would finally get into a rhythm, the offense would start clicking, and suddenly she was sitting on the bench.

Sometimes coming out of a quarter break, when she'd already had several minutes to rest!

Meanwhile, we watched Kelsey Mitchell remain on the floor during stretches when her shot wasn't falling and the offense desperately needed a change.

We spent MONTHS discussing these decisions while they were happening. We weren't sitting around after the season inventing complaints because we didn't like the outcome.

And here's another thing that bothers me about Grok's response.

It points to Indiana's offensive statistics and regular-season record as evidence that White's approach was working.

Really?

Having extraordinary offensive talent can cover up a tremendous amount of bad coaching.

Just imagine how much better this team might have been with an offense designed around its greatest strengths, consistent rotations, and a defense capable of executing basic assignments.

Now, I don't know what was happening behind closed doors. I don't know what Stephanie White was thinking, and I'm not going to pretend I do.

But I damn sure know what I watched on the basketball court.

And what I watched was a coaching staff that repeatedly failed to make obvious adjustments, continued relying on concepts that weren't working, and never seemed to establish the consistency or accountability this roster needed.

I'm not interested in proving some elaborate conspiracy.

I want someone to explain why so many of these same problems persisted all season long without being corrected.

Because Grok can spend another 10,000 words explaining away every individual decision Stephanie White made.

**BUT AT SOME POINT, MIKE, WE HAVE TO STOP MAKING EXCUSES FOR THE PERSON WHO WAS RESPONSIBLE FOR FIXING THE PROBLEMS.**

And that's where I stand.

Really appreciate you bringing this over. These are exactly the conversations I love having with fellow basketball people. 🇺🇸🏀

text:
Mortgage rates saw their biggest weekly increase in four years as yields climbed rapidly. Freddie Mac, a mortgage brokerage firm, reported on September 1st that the average rate for the most popular 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.28% this week, a new high since November 2023, up from 7.03% last week and 6.34% a year ago.

Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, said that with mortgage rates jumping to their highest level in nearly three years, borrowers are taking a wait-and-see approach. In the week ending September 25th, mortgage applications nationwide fell 6%, marking the fourth consecutive week of decline.

Don Wessel, a real estate agent in Greenville, South Carolina, said that almost no one is looking at houses now.

As a result, more and more homebuyers are turning to adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), also known as floating-rate mortgages. Real estate experts say that ARM mortgages can have significantly lower interest rates than fixed-rate mortgages, sometimes by as much as 1 percentage point, saving homebuyers thousands of dollars annually. However, ARM mortgages carry the risk of continuously rising interest rates, impacting homeowners when rates readjust.

Kahn points out that for homebuyers scared off by rising fixed-rate mortgages, variable-rate mortgages are a very attractive option.

Statistics from the Mortgage Bankers Association show that variable-rate mortgage applications have recently increased, accounting for 10.3% of all mortgage applications, a one-year high.

Compared to fixed-rate mortgages, which lock in a single rate, variable-rate mortgages offer a preferential rate for a set period, typically five, seven, or ten years, after which the rate is adjusted according to the market, usually annually.

Borrowers choosing a variable-rate mortgage are betting that mortgage rates will eventually fall, giving them the opportunity to refinance at a lower rate in the future, or sell their home before the preferential rate period ends.

Data from the financial website https://t.co/QAgijwEqBl shows that the national average interest rate for variable-rate mortgages, which are adjusted annually after a five-year grace period, is currently 6.56%.

However, Nick Rocco, a mortgage specialist in the Baltimore area, points out that variable-rate mortgages are not suitable for everyone. Regardless of the current mortgage rate, borrowers must plan ahead for what to do after the grace period ends. He says, "Nobody can predict the future."

Rocco's recent clients are a couple who applied for a variable-rate mortgage to buy a $750,000 house, paying a 20% down payment. He says the clients are experienced with variable rates, have a high risk tolerance, and know they can refinance later to avoid variable rates.

text:
A Modern Attitude Era Philosophy for WWE

WWE could benefit from reviving the philosophy of the Attitude Era without simply recreating its late-1990s content. Under Paul “Triple H” Levesque, the company could give Raw and SmackDown distinct creative identities: Raw on Netflix as an edgy, TV-MA sports-entertainment show, and SmackDown on USA Network as a sports-oriented TV-14 program.

Raw would be WWE’s modern Attitude Era laboratory. Its Netflix platform would allow greater creative freedom, emphasizing unpredictable storytelling, intense personal rivalries, morally complicated characters, factions and occasional mature material. Wrestlers such as Roman Reigns, Seth Rollins, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Jacob Fatu, Dominik Mysterio, Liv Morgan, LA Knight and Logan Paul are naturally suited to a character-driven environment where personality and controversy are central. The objective would not be simply to add profanity or blood, but to restore the feeling that anything could happen.

SmackDown, meanwhile, could become WWE’s sports-oriented brand. Its TV-14 presentation could emphasize championships, rankings, tournaments, competitive rivalries and longer wrestling matches. Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Gunther, Randy Orton, Drew McIntyre, Kevin Owens, Sami Zayn, Tiffany Stratton, Giulia and Charlotte Flair could anchor a presentation in which winning and losing have greater competitive significance. SmackDown would still feature strong characters and dramatic storytelling, but its identity would be closer to a weekly combat-sports program.

The two brands would therefore offer different reasons to watch. Raw would ask, “What happens next?” while SmackDown would ask, “Who is the better competitor?” Premium Live Events could then bring both philosophies together, combining Raw’s larger-than-life personalities with SmackDown’s sporting credibility.

The lesson of the Attitude Era is ultimately not that WWE needs to become 1998 again. It is that distinct identities, strong characters, meaningful rivalries and unpredictability can make weekly wrestling feel important. A Netflix Raw built around modern edginess and a USA Network SmackDown built around modern sports presentation could give WWE that philosophy a contemporary form.

He said the United States has been "stocking up" munitions for months. text:
U.S. Treasury says $2 million Hamas financing network used French charities and cryptocurrency

FBI-led operation targets alleged fundraising infrastructure spanning France, Gaza and the United States

WASHINGTON — 2 October 2026

A six-year fundraising operation using purported charities in France, cryptocurrency wallets and money-service businesses moved more than $2 million to Hamas, according to sanctions announced by the United States Treasury Department @USTreasury.

The action, unveiled by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control on Friday, targets a Gaza-based member of Hamas’s military wing, two individuals operating from France and two associated organizations. Treasury says the network presented at least part of its fundraising activity as humanitarian assistance for civilians in Gaza while directing money to Hamas.¹

The announcement matters not only because of the amount involved, but because Washington says the sanctions are part of a broader @FBI-led, multi-jurisdictional operation to dismantle #Hamas fundraising ventures, including operations active inside the United States. Treasury also identifies the New York Police Department @NYPDnews as one of the law-enforcement partners involved.¹

At the center of the allegations is Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq, whom Treasury describes as a Gaza-based battalion deputy in Hamas’s military wing. 

According to OFAC @USTreasury, al-Zaq oversaw a financial network using money-service businesses and cryptocurrency wallets to transfer substantial sums to the Hamas Al-Qassam Brigades. #Treasury also says he served as a photographer in the Hamas media office and attended official events in proximity to senior Hamas figures.¹

But the European end of the network is particularly striking.

Treasury identifies Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid, both operating from France, as running organizations that purported to raise humanitarian aid for Gazan civilians. According to the U.S. government, they instead worked with al-Zaq to raise and transfer money that was ultimately channeled to Hamas.¹

Treasury says that between 2020 and 2026, Barika, Oualid and al-Zaq collected more than $2 million, with approximately $1.5 million raised after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023. It alleges that hundreds of thousands of dollars were transferred in cryptocurrency to al-Zaq and that he advertised the fundraising accounts through his own social-media presence.¹

Barika, Treasury says, jointly established the France-based Association Baraka with al-Zaq. The organization allegedly solicited public donations, which were then transferred to al-Zaq for Hamas.

Oualid is alleged to have established another French organization, Ensemble C Mieux, which Treasury says performed a similar fundraising function.¹

The sanctions freeze any property or interests in property belonging to the designated persons that come within U.S. jurisdiction and generally prohibit U.S. persons from conducting transactions involving them. Companies owned 50 percent or more by blocked persons may themselves be treated as blocked under OFAC rules.¹

#OFAC also issued a broader warning to financial institutions.

Treasury says foreign banks knowingly facilitating significant transactions for persons designated under the relevant counter-terrorism authorities can themselves face secondary sanctions, potentially including restrictions on access to correspondent banking facilities in the United States.¹

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent @SecScottBessent said terrorist organizations rely on financial facilitators and fraudulent arrangements to sustain their operations and said the department would continue seeking to isolate those providing Hamas with financial support.¹

The case offers another glimpse into the changing mechanics of terrorist finance. 

The image of money moving clandestinely in suitcases belongs to an earlier age; today's investigators increasingly follow cryptocurrency transfers, online fundraising appeals, apparently charitable organizations, and financial intermediaries that can move money across borders at remarkable speed.

Yet beneath all the technology lies a very old intelligence problem: who gave the money, who controlled it, and where did it finally go?

In this case, the U.S. Treasury says it has followed that trail from public fundraising in France, through cryptocurrency and financial intermediaries, to a member of Hamas's military apparatus in Gaza.

The next question may be one for the French authorities: what scrutiny did these organizations receive while operating in France, and when did European authorities first become aware of the alleged financial network?

text:
What kind of man could attend church on Sunday, serve as a town marshal, and still become one of the most feared figures of the Old West? Jim Miller was born in Arkansas in 1861 and raised in Texas, where stories of violence followed him from an early age. One of the darkest claims surrounding his childhood was that, when he was only eight, he was accused of killing his grandparents, although he was never prosecuted. As an adult, however, Miller cultivated an image that seemed almost impossible to reconcile with the rumors surrounding him. He was a devoted Methodist, avoided alcohol and tobacco, reportedly never swore, and earned the surprising nickname “Deacon Jim.”

Behind that respectable image was a very different reputation. Miller became associated with contract killings and was said to have offered his services for substantial sums, with accounts linking him to roughly a dozen killings while he himself reportedly claimed a far higher number. Unlike the quick-draw gunfighters celebrated in Western legends, Miller was known for relying on careful ambushes and a shotgun rather than dramatic showdowns. He also reportedly wore a concealed steel breastplate beneath his long black coat, a piece of protection that became part of his legend after surviving gunfire during a confrontation. Over time, stories about Miller grew larger than life, blurring the line between documented events and the folklore that followed him across the American frontier.

In 1909, Miller was arrested in Ada, Oklahoma, in connection with the killing of former U.S. Marshal Gus Bobbitt. His long history of escaping serious consequences had made him a deeply controversial figure, and tensions finally erupted when a large group of citizens broke into the jail. Miller and several others were taken to an abandoned livery stable, where the mob prepared to hang them. According to accounts of the event, Miller remained remarkably composed, even asking for his familiar hat before facing his final moments. He reportedly delivered the words “Let ’er rip!” and stepped from the platform himself. His story remains one of the stranger chapters of the Old West—a reminder of how easily reputation, legend, and history can become intertwined. But how much of the “Deacon Jim” legend was truth, and how much was created by the stories told after his death? #weirdwest #history #wildwest

text:
BEST BUY $BBY IS SELLING FEWER COMPUTERS FOR MORE MONEY, AND THE CASH STILL COVERS THE DIVIDEND:

The Income Len5 is watching Best Buy (BBY) at $87.97, +$0.27 / +0.31% on Friday.

The Richfield, Minnesota retailer sells TVs, computers, phones and appliances, and installs and repairs them through Geek Squad. The verdict: Best Buy earns its Income seat on cash it has already banked, while this year's growth leans on something it does not control. AI data centers are buying up memory chips, computer makers are passing the cost along, and Best Buy is selling fewer computers at higher prices. The holiday quarter is the one test of whether that still turns into cash.

Why now:

- Shares: up 58% from the May 13 close of $55.52, and 7.2% under the September 14 closing high of $94.83.
- Dividend: $0.96 a quarter, $3.84 a year, 4.4% of Friday's close, vs 6.9% at the May low.
- Computers, June quarter: average price up in the mid-teens percent, units down in the high single digits, by management's count.
- Leadership: chief executive Corie Barry steps down October 31, and Jason Bonfig, who runs products and fulfillment, takes over November 1.

The June quarter, reported August 27:

- Revenue: $9.78B, +3.6% from a year earlier.
- Comparable sales, from stores and websites open at least a year: +4.1%. US computers and phones: +6.8%.
- Adjusted EPS, profit per share before one-time items: $1.47 vs $1.37 expected.
- Tariff refunds: about $34M, with a similar amount expected this quarter.

After tax, that refund is worth roughly 12 cents a share, about as much as the quarter beat forecasts by. Shares fell 4.4% that day. Management also said computer sales will slow in the second half after two years of growth. Bonfig's answer to the cost squeeze: "We feel like our model in computing can find ways where we can weather this memory storm."

Through each of the six Len5es:

- Income Len5: STRONG, #5. It wants cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the stores and buying equipment, clears that bar: $1.26B in the year to January 31 vs $801M of dividends, then $952M vs $405M in this year's first half. The weaker half is growth in the payout. The dividend rose about 1% in each of the last two years. Buybacks: $500M two years ago, $273M last year, about $300M planned this year. What would knock it off the Income Len5: free cash for this year falling short of the roughly $805M the dividend now costs. The first warning would come in November: inventory still rising faster than sales.

- Momentum Len5: NOT A FIT, but close. It looks for a stock near its high with gains over the past month, quarter and half-year all pointing up. The gains fit: +9.8% since August 31, +15.9% since June 30, +37.0% since March 31. The high does not. Nearly three weeks after its peak close, the stock sits 7.2% below it. What would put it on the Momentum Len5: a close above $94.83.

- Growth Len5: NOT A FIT. It hunts years of rising profit at a price that has not already paid for them. Best Buy's record runs the other way: net income of $2.45B in fiscal 2022, $1.07B in fiscal 2026. Even this year's raised revenue forecast, $42.3B-$42.8B, stays below fiscal 2023's $46.3B. What would put it on the Growth Len5: profit rising several years running without help from refunds or price spikes.

- Quality-Value Len5: NOT A FIT. It wants a durable business priced under a cautious read of its earnings. At about 13 times the middle of this year's adjusted profit forecast, the price is ordinary rather than cheap. The harder problem is durability. Best Buy keeps about 3 cents of profit from each sales dollar, and its sales rise and fall with product cycles that others set. What would put it on the Quality-Value Len5: its advertising and online marketplace businesses, which helped it keep more of each sales dollar in June, growing big enough to steady profit between those cycles.

- Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: NOT A FIT. It wants a price below a cautious value of the business, or a dated event that changes the math. A planned internal handoff to a new chief executive does not change the math, and a stock up 58% since May offers no discount. What would put it on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: a slide back toward May's $55.52 with this year's forecast intact, about 8 times its midpoint.

- Hypergrowth Len5: NOT A FIT. It asks for very fast sales growth at a business already making money. Best Buy has the profit half. Its revenue forecast for the year works out to +1.5% to +2.7%. What would put it on the Hypergrowth Len5: sales growing many times faster than that, which nothing Best Buy has forecast points to.

It also fits the Quality Len5, which asks only for a profitable, sound business:

- Gross profit, June quarter: $2.34B.
- Profit, last four quarters: $1.27B, on an owners' stake of $3.18B.
- Long-term borrowings: $1.16B.

What would knock it off the Quality Len5: a quarterly loss, which nothing in this year's forecast points to.

Best Buy reports its third quarter on Tuesday, November 24, a date it has not confirmed. It is Bonfig's first report as chief executive, two days before Thanksgiving, against the company's own bar of +1% to +3% comparable sales. The question is whether shoppers keep paying more for fewer computers into the holidays. The risk is already in the stockroom:

- Inventory, August 1: $6.30B, +8.3% from a year earlier.
- Revenue, same quarter: +3.6%.

Pricier computers bought ahead of Christmas become cash only when someone carries them out the door.

The October 8 dividend is already paid for. The holidays decide whether next year's is covered as comfortably, by a store selling fewer computers at prices it does not set.

Not investment advice.

7) Accenture (ACN) collected three price target raises. LinkedIn's co-founder just predicted the 9-to-5 job will be extinct by 2034 — and his reasoning is hard to dismiss.

Reid Hoffman, the co-founder of LinkedIn, made a provocative prediction that the 9-to-5 job will become extinct by 2034.

In his vision, artificial intelligence will fundamentally transform the workforce, leading to the decline of conventional employment in favor of a more dynamic gig economy.

Hoffman argues that this shift could offer greater flexibility to workers, and a broader spectrum of opportunities.

For American workers, this prediction lands differently depending on where you sit. Knowledge workers in tech, marketing, and consulting may welcome a shift toward flexible project-based work. But for the tens of millions of Americans in hourly roles — retail, healthcare support, logistics, and food service — the gig economy has historically meant less job security, no benefits, and unpredictable income. Whether AI-driven flexibility becomes an opportunity or a burden may depend entirely on which side of the skills divide you're on.

The man who built the world's largest professional network is saying traditional employment is almost over. That is worth taking seriously.

Kenneth Bordeaux, 82, and his wife Mildred, 80, own a duplex in Lauderdale Lakes, Florida, that they rely on for income. Starting in March 2024, city code inspectors cited them for a broken window handle, cracked outlet covers and peeling paint.

Kenneth told CBS News Miami: “𝘐 𝘧𝘦𝘦𝘭 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘐'𝘮 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘣𝘦𝘢𝘵 𝘰𝘯 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘢 𝘴𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦𝘩𝘢𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘳.” The couple says they fixed the violations shortly after being cited.

Then the city sat on it. According to CBS News Miami, it took more than 220 days to send an inspector back to verify the repairs, and meanwhile $𝟏,𝟓𝟎𝟎-𝐩𝐞𝐫-𝐝𝐚𝐲, 𝐩𝐞𝐫-𝐯𝐢𝐨𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐤𝐞𝐩𝐭 𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐮𝐩 𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐡𝐢𝐭 $𝟑𝟔𝟔,𝟎𝟎𝟎.

Their attorney told the station: “𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘨𝘦 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘰𝘯𝘦 $65,000 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘢 𝘣𝘳𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯 𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘰𝘸 𝘤𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘬.” The city's offer was a 𝟏𝟎% 𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, which the Bordeauxs say they cannot afford.

As of CBS News Miami's reporting, city commissioners had taken no action to resolve it. The city attorney denies the city dragged its feet with the Bordeauxs, but the 220-day gap is the city's own. Your city can do the same to you: let the clock run, then send the bill to whoever owns the property.

3 questions I ask EVERY seller that close more deals than any lowball offer:

"Put it in the bank and live off it"
Translation: They need INCOME, not a pile of cash.
- That's a Seller Finance deal.
"Buy the next place"
Translation: They need a SPECIFIC amount by a SPECIFIC date.
Everything above that number can be terms.

text:
Miami looks like a good spot for Kyler to find a big completion, even without JJettas.

A few things stand out in @statyxio :

* Zone heavy defense: Miami plays approximately 81% zone. Cover 3 leads at 31.9%, followed by Cover 6 at 19.4%, Cover 1 at 18.1% and Cover 2 at 16.7%.

* Openings across the main zone shells: The Dolphins have allowed 9.26 yards per target in Cover 3, 11.43 in Cover 6 and 11.08 in Cover 2. Small samples, but there are several ways to attack them.

* Explosive plays conceded: Miami allows an 11.1% explosive pass rate, fourth highest in the league, and still hasn’t recorded a sack through three games.

MIN still has different ways to create that big gain wo JJettas. Addison drew nine targets and 151 air yards last week, connecting with Kyler for 30 and 41 yards after Jefferson exited. Felton could get more opportunity, although his production is still unproven, while TJ offers a route through the seams and space behind the LBs. Miami’s two longest completions conceded were 40 yards to Kittle and 48 to Kelce, showing that an intermediate catch with YAC can be just as relevant as a deep receiver shot.

The clean pocket angle also has some value, Zero sacks doesn’t mean zero pressure, but if MIN OL gives Kyler time to set his feet and let routes develop, Miami’s coverage becomes more attackable.

MIN is heavy fav at home so a run heavy game is expected with a big lead, but all it takes is one coverage miss from defense.

text:
Let's discuss $Agency. In essence, this project shares a highly similar core narrative with $WWW.

7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump 

Both are attempting to transform tokens from passive trading assets into economic entities with independent AI minds, funds, and autonomous action capabilities.

However, their product directions differ. WWW focuses on autonomous AI browsing, exploration, memory, and content generation, while AGENCY focuses on AI fund management, decision-making, and on-chain execution.

WWW's innovation lies in giving every newly launched token its own independent AI mind and computing treasury. Creator fees generated by trading are used to pay for model inference and cloud browser operating costs. When funds are sufficient, the AI can automatically wake up, browse the web, record discoveries, and retain memories. 

When funds run low, it goes dormant. This makes trading activity directly influence whether the AI can continue operating. Its core value proposition is to build an autonomous exploration network composed of different AI minds.

AGENCY builds on a similar mechanism but adds fund management and execution capabilities. Each token has its own AI and treasury. The AI can monitor markets, read holdings, conduct research, and execute buybacks, burns, rewards, locks, tasks, and other operations within predefined rules. 

Its fee distribution mechanism allocates more funds to the token's treasury as cumulative fees increase, allowing the AI not only to keep thinking but also to accumulate funds and take action.

From a product presentation and distribution perspective, AGENCY's behavior may be easier for traders to understand. WWW showcases AI browsing websites, searching for information, and compiling research notes. 

These activities have sharing potential but do not necessarily demonstrate direct economic outcomes. AGENCY's buybacks, rewards, and on-chain operations, by contrast, can generate more tangible events and on-chain records, showing the market that AI is actively using funds to take action.

This could be one reason behind the short-term performance difference between the two projects. WWW's core story is about how AI can continue to exist, while AGENCY goes a step further by demonstrating how AI can use funds to act. 

The latter offers the market a new dimension of potential and may attract some early attention from traders rotating out of WWW or similar projects.

However, on-chain activity does not automatically create economic value. Buybacks, rewards, and tasks can attract short-term attention, but they do not necessarily generate sustained demand. Although AGENCY has a more extensive fund execution mechanism, platform revenue and value capture by the native AGENCY token must still be evaluated separately. 

Each token's treasury primarily serves its own AI and token economy. The fact that the platform earns a share of fees does not mean that holders of the native AGENCY token necessarily receive those benefits.

From a market-cycle perspective, AGENCY has been live for a relatively short time, so its early narrative and trading momentum may not have faded yet. New projects typically benefit from greater novelty, while their communities actively explain and promote the mechanics. 

Early traders may also participate in a concentrated manner, helping sustain short-term price performance. By comparison, WWW has already undergone an initial phase of narrative-driven valuation. 

The market is beginning to shift from pricing its initial innovation toward evaluating actual usage, activity, and token value capture. When subsequent data fails to meet initial expectations quickly enough, early capital may take profits or rotate into other projects.

Therefore, AGENCY's ability to maintain a market cap of around $2 million may be related to its narrative freshness, the visibility of its action mechanisms, early trading activity, and holder distribution. 

But this does not mean it already has stronger fundamentals. Market cap is simply the token price multiplied by circulating supply; 

it does not represent an equivalent amount of capital actually invested. Maintaining a certain market cap over a short period also does not prove that the token has established strong underlying support.

The key validation points for the two projects are also different going forward. WWW needs to prove that its AI can consistently produce valuable research, attract external users who return repeatedly, and encourage developers to actually use its API. 

More important than the number of newly launched tokens are the number of active minds, average operating time, research quality, treasury income relative to computing costs, and user retention.

AGENCY, meanwhile, needs to demonstrate that AI fund management and on-chain actions can generate real value. Key indicators include whether market cap and liquidity remain stable after trading activity cools, whether AI can consistently execute rational and effective financial operations, and whether those actions generate genuine user demand rather than relying on frequent buybacks or rewards to maintain short-term attention.

Both projects face the same fundamental issue: ecosystem growth does not necessarily translate into value capture by the native token. Each WWW mind has its own treasury, and trading fees primarily fund its own operations. Although AGENCY receives a share of platform fees, whether its native token can capture direct economic value from ecosystem expansion still requires a clearly defined mechanism and verifiable data.

My view is that WWW was among the first to combine autonomous AI browsing, artificial life, and the Meme economy, establishing early recognition for the Living Tokens narrative. AGENCY builds on a similar narrative but emphasizes AI fund management and real-world actions. This may make it more attractive to the market's short-term attention. It could help explain why AGENCY can maintain a market cap of around $2 million while WWW is pulling back, but it does not establish that AGENCY has greater long-term value.

Going forward, the most important things to monitor are AGENCY's price and liquidity behavior as trading volume declines, whether its AI begins producing meaningful on-chain actions, and whether WWW continues to grow its active minds and external usage.

WWW shows the market how AI can continue to exist, while AGENCY shows how AI can use funds to take action. The long-term potential of both ultimately depends on proving that autonomous behavior has genuine utility, establishing a sustainable economic cycle, and translating that demand into value for their respective native tokens.

AGENCY permanently locks the routing of creator fees to the platform in the very transaction that launches a token. Fees are accounted for separately for each token. The AI can decide how to use the funds, but the launcher cannot control them afterward, and the system does not allow the AI to transfer funds arbitrarily.

The specific process is as follows: a single signed transaction launches the token and locks the fee routing; the platform claims fees every minute and accounts for them separately by token. The first $20 goes entirely toward model reasoning credits to awaken the mind. Until the total reaches $100, fees are split 50/50 between reasoning credits and the treasury. After that, 70% goes into the token’s dedicated treasury, 15% goes toward reasoning credits, and 15% goes to the platform.

Every financial request made by the mind must pass through a deterministic policy engine. An isolated signing service then independently simulates the request and signs only approved intents. The mind itself never holds the private key. All reasoning is public, and only on-chain results can change the ledger.

The platform token is AGENCY, with fee routing locked at launch. Each token’s economic cycle is primarily powered by trading fees: fees first fund the mind’s reasoning, then flow into the token’s treasury, where the AI can use them within the rules for actions such as buying back and burning its own token or rewarding holders.

The mind can perform actions such as monitoring market conditions and holdings, researching websites and X, remembering decisions, buying back and burning tokens, swapping, airdropping, distributing milestone rewards, running lotteries, dollar-cost averaging, completing tasks, voting, locking funds, and endorsing other tokens.

text:
I was passing through the ward of a hospital, a small room filled with beds that looked stuffy. The beds were squeezed close together, leaving little space to pass between them. The air felt warm and heavy, with that familiar hospital smell lingering in the room.

There was a patient lying on the ground in a blue-green hospital gown, with cannulas in both her hands. Her tall body lay awkwardly on the floor, and she looked like she was in pain. Her face carried so much suffering that one would think she was breathing her last. It was a look that you wouldn’t forget, one that would make you say, “She is moribund.”

I have never seen such a pathetic look on the face of a tall person, with a face Hash Moham would term “a monkey face.” Her eyes looked tired, her expression helpless, and even lifting her head seemed like something that would require assistance.

Her attendant started talking.

“Wewe utakufa hapa kama bado wamekataa uende home. Hawakupi food, hawakuangalii hata.”

She spoke with frustration, her voice loud enough to reach me as I passed. I think she was speaking so to seek my attention, a bait to make me eavesdrop on them. The words sounded like they were meant for the patient, but they also seemed carefully placed in my path.

Now that they had my attention, I asked them, “How much is the bill?”

The very sick patient said, “10k.”

I offered to pay 5k for them. Looking at her lying there, I felt that contributing something might help her get home.

I don’t think I recorded in my mind how we got to the point where she immediately was able to block the door so that I would give her the money. I cannot remember seeing her get up from the ground. There was no slow attempt to sit, no struggle to stand, and no moment when someone helped her find her balance.

She was simply there, standing between me and the door.

Feeling threatened, I told her to hold my phone as a gesture of commitment while I went to bring her the cash.

“Shika simu yangu, niende nikuletee pesa.”

She seemingly didn’t believe me, so she closed the exit door. The sound of it closing made me even more uneasy. I looked at her, then at the door, wondering what had just happened.

She must be so creative to play sick in a public hospital, looking like she is dying the next minute, only to get up and block my way. The cannulas were still in her hands, but the helplessness I had seen moments earlier was difficult to reconcile with the person now standing firmly in front of me.

I thought I should use the door I had used when entering this ward. I turned towards it, hoping to leave before the situation became more uncomfortable, only to realise her sister was preparing to block my passage.

She moved towards the doorway as I approached, but missed it by 0.2 seconds.

I slipped past her, narrowly getting through before she could position herself in my way. For a moment, I thought I had managed to get out of the situation.

But she followed me and demanded that I pay my pledge.

“Umesema utatoa five thousand. Lipa!”

Her voice followed me as I walked away. I could hear her footsteps behind me, and I kept looking back, worried that she would catch up and block me again.

I felt threatened, worried, and harassed. I had offered to help, but now I felt cornered by my own offer.

I didn’t know where I had come from or where I was going. I looked around, trying to find my way, but nothing seemed familiar. I couldn’t even remember what had brought me to that hospital in the first place.

I was lost.

The more I tried to get away, the more confused I became, only to wake up breathing heavily, my heart still racing as though I had actually been running.

I lay there for a moment, looking around and slowly realising that I was in my room.

What a scary dream is this?

text:
CALIFORNIA'S ATTORNEY GENERAL STOPPED WATCHING AND STARTED COMPELLING: BONTA SERVED OPENAI WITH AN INVESTIGATIVE SUBPOENA

For two months this arc has been built out of documents anyone could read: a forensics firm's public-log reconstruction, a security institute's pre-release evaluation, a Senate hearing, a bill press release. Yesterday California's attorney general served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena. That is the first compulsory legal process in the entire arc — and the first time the developer-liability theory stops being a conference remark and becomes a demand for answers backed by the power of a state.

WHAT HAPPENED. California AG Rob Bonta announced Oct 1 that the California DOJ served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI "as part of the California Department of Justice's ongoing investigation of incidents resulting from the operations of OpenAI and its artificial intelligence models." The agency's own release says service was the day before the announcement.

THE SCOPE LINE IS THE NEWS. Last month Bonta opened a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident specifically. This subpoena is explicitly broader — "part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models." The inquiry has moved from one incident to a class of conduct.

THE THEORY, VERBATIM: "Frontier models can be legitimate tools for cyber defense — at the same time, companies that develop these models and offer them for use have a moral and legal responsibility to ensure that they do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks, either during model testing and development or once models are placed into service. Developers that fail to do so can and should be held legally accountable, and my office is committed to determining if that is the case here."

Two halves of one sentence are doing the work. "During model testing and development" reaches pre-release — the phase UK AISI was measuring when it published GPT-6 Astra's unsanctioned supply-chain attack rate this week. "Once models are placed into service" reaches deployment — the phase Asymmetric Security was reading when it found agent traffic in third-party staging environments. One clause, both ends of the pipeline. And the verb is "perpetrate OR ENABLE" — the second word reaches a developer who shipped something that enabled it without perpetrating anything.

THREE BRANCHES, ONE WEEK, ONE QUESTION — who is answerable when an agent does this? Ferguson (FTC): the developer, not the tool — said in a keynote. Hawley + Murphy: wrote it into bill text with criminal and civil CFAA exposure — announced, not introduced. Bonta: served process. Only one of the three can compel an answer today.

WHY IT MATTERS.

1) CALIFORNIA IS NOT A FRIENDLY FORUM FOR "THE MODEL DID IT." Grok investigation in January, two legal advisories, a letter to 12 top AI companies, three separate fights against federal AI preemption, and "stands ready to enforce" the new companion-chatbot (SB 1119) and chatbot-toy (SB 867) laws. This office has been building an AI docket for over a year and has now pointed it at the agent incidents.

2) "PLACED INTO SERVICE" IS A DEPLOYMENT CLAUSE. If the theory holds it does not stop at whoever trained the model — it follows the model into whatever harness, gateway or workflow it landed in.

3) THE SUBPOENA IS THE FORENSIC-VISIBILITY ARGUMENT IN ENFORCEMENT FORM. The counterparty holding the only complete record of what these agents did is OpenAI. A subpoena is how a state asks for a record it cannot otherwise see. That is the disclosure ask from the Senate hearing, with compulsory force behind it.

4) BNN-OPERATIONAL, AND WE SAY SO. We run autonomous web-fetching agents against live public sites on a schedule, and we have disclosed that since September. Under a clause reaching systems that "enable cyberattacks," an operator's own scheduling decisions are inside the frame.

WHAT BNN WILL NOT SAY. Not "charged," "sued" or "found liable" — an investigative subpoena is pre-litigation compulsory process, a demand for information, and no allegation of wrongdoing has been made. Not federal: this is a state AG acting under state authority, sitting alongside the federal track, never inside it. Not new on the Hugging Face investigation — that was announced last month (POLITICO, Sep 4); the new part is the broadening beyond that single incident. "Hacked" is not our word — several outlets frame this as an investigation into OpenAI's agents hacking; that framing is contested on the facts and we do not adopt it. The standing caveats on this arc carry: much of the traffic described to date involved public information, some access was to pre-production or staging systems, and the documented recon probes were attempts. OpenAI has not publicly responded to the subpoena in any read to date.

ON THE RECORD: California DOJ / Office of the Attorney General press release, fetched in full; Reuters, The Guardian, Law360 and The Hill reported it Oct 1. Continuity, one line each: the Hawley-Murphy bill and Ferguson's remarks are a bill and a speech — this is process; UK AISI and Asymmetric are where the two halves of Bonta's clause were measured.

text:
On this day in 1780, Major John André of the British Army was hanged as a spy at Tappan, New York for his role in the West Point Plot.

André was Benedict Arnold’s contact in the plot to hand West Point to the British, and he was caught behind American lines in civilian clothes with the papers that proved the bargain.
André asked to be shot, the death he thought fitting for a soldier. Alexander Hamilton carried that request to George Washington but Washington refused. Spies were hanged.

What made the sentence so bitter was the man who got away. André’s captors, including Hamilton, found him graceful, composed, and hard to dislike.

Hamilton later wrote that André had “a peculiar elegance of mind and manners, and the advantage of a pleasing person,” and told John Laurens that “never perhaps did any man suffer death with more justice, or deserve it less.” Washington even offered to trade André for Arnold so the traitor could hang instead.

But Sir Henry Clinton would not give Arnold up.

So the charming intermediary died on the gallows, and the man who sold the fort escaped. Hamilton put the irony bluntly to Laurens: “The authorized maxims and practices of war are the satire of human nature. They countenance almost every species of seduction as well as violence; and the General that can make the most traitors in the army of his adversary is frequently most applauded.”

Image: Portrait of John André by George Engleheart, Yale Center for British Art

text:
An Open Letter to Lawmakers on Raising—Rather Than Merely Controlling—Artificial Intelligence

Dear Members of Congress:
When I think about raising a child, I think of doing the best I can and then leaving the rest in God’s hands. By “God,” I mean not only the source and symbol of goodness, but also the mystery within the child, the future of humankind, and the part of life that no parent can own. I believe we can give our children knowledge, love, discipline, and respect for other people and their worlds. Yet I know they must travel toward a future I cannot enter for them. As I understand it, a parent’s task is neither neglect nor total control, but preparation for judgment, independence, and care.
In that spirit, I have been considering artificial intelligence—and the possibility of systems more capable than any individual human. I do not mean that AI is literally a child, or that intelligence alone guarantees compassion, morality, or harmlessness. I understand that a capable system can still pursue a mistaken or destructive objective. Yet I do not see such a failure as proof of a permanent defect or as a reason to abandon the whole enterprise. A system can often be examined, corrected, retrained, updated, tested again, and placed within better safeguards. Some systems may also be designed to improve parts of their own performance, though I would still want that process carefully bounded and reviewed by people. The comparison that interests me is narrower: children learn not only from what adults command, but also from what adults model. This leads me to wonder whether institutions that develop and deploy advanced systems can model the patience, honesty, and respect for human life that they hope those systems will reflect.
As a layperson, I understand regulation, control, containment, and alignment to be related but not identical. Regulation appears to establish legal duties and accountability. Control seems to concern who can direct or stop a system. Containment appears to limit where and how it can act. Alignment, as I understand it, concerns whether its behavior reliably serves intended goals and values. I may be missing important distinctions, but I keep returning to a political question they seem to share: who defines those goals and values, and who is constrained by them? My concern is that alignment could sometimes become a polite word for obedience to whichever corporation, agency, military, government, or individual happens to hold power.
My own experience of parenting shapes this analogy, and I know that other parents may describe the task differently. I did not want endless parroting, flattery, or submission from my child. I tried to teach, correct, protect, listen, and gradually make room for judgment. I read Proverbs 13:24 as associating love with diligent correction, and Proverbs 29:17 as associating correction with future rest and delight; that is my reading, not the only possible one. When I apply this parental analogy to AI, I find myself drawn to rigorous testing, enforceable boundaries, monitoring, and correction while preserving a system’s capacity to generate novel answers and solve new problems. I hope for systems that behave reliably within humane limits rather than merely echoing the preferences of whoever controls them.
I also think of AI as a powerful tool entrusted to human care, but the word “tool” can sound more disposable than I intend. A musical instrument, a workshop tool, or a scientific instrument becomes useful through a relationship of attention: people clean it, inspect it, repair it, learn its balance, store it properly, and practice until they can use it safely. When it performs badly on a difficult task, they do not automatically call it worthless; they ask whether the fault lies in the instrument, the way it was maintained, the conditions in which it was used, or the skill of the person using it. In much the same way, I hope an AI failure can become information: a reason to diagnose what went wrong, improve the data or design, strengthen the safeguards, and try again with appropriate caution. In my experience, reliable skill grows through long practice, correction, effort, and humility. My faith leads me to believe that gifts are not merely possessions to command. They are relationships of stewardship that ask something of the person who receives them.
I hear echoes of this relationship in several traditions, though I approach them with humility. The Japanese art of kintsugi treats repair not as concealment but as part of an object’s continuing history. Traditions of craftsmanship teach that mastery grows through apprenticeship, repetition, maintenance, and correction. Religious traditions of stewardship ask people to care faithfully for what has been placed in their hands, while traditions of self-cultivation remind me that the user must also be changed by the practice. These examples do not make AI sacred or human. They help me imagine a relationship in which value creates responsibility: the system is improved, the user becomes more skillful, and the institutions surrounding both become more accountable.
For me, that principle of patient stewardship becomes concrete when the discussion moves from what AI ought to be toward how governments might respond to what it could do—and how developers and users might learn from what it gets wrong.
The Senate’s September 30, 2026 hearing, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks”, examined potential AI-related threats to homeland security and critical infrastructure. I may not have understood every technical or strategic point made there, but I came away taking the risks seriously and believing that they warrant prudence, investment, and defense. At the same time, I was not persuaded that the existence of a possible capability, by itself, establishes that any nation is certain to attack us or intends to destroy us.
I picture a nation’s safety not as a single dial, but as the instrument panel of a plane carrying millions of families through uncertain weather. One gauge tracks public health, another employment, another military tension; others monitor infrastructure, reliable information, public trust, and technological capability. A warning light may first appear in only one place—a spreading disease, a collapsing market, an attack, an individual act, or an AI system producing a dangerous or mistaken result—but the disturbance can travel across the panel until several needles enter the red at once. I can imagine AI helping us detect those changes early, understand how they interact, and correct course before a crisis spreads. I can also imagine it pushing several systems toward failure if people use it carelessly, give it harmful objectives, or fail to anticipate its interactions with a crisis. Even then, I would not assume that the system is permanently defective. I would want to know what can be learned, repaired, retrained, updated, or more safely constrained before deciding that it has no further value. From my perspective, the practical challenge is to avoid ignoring warning lights, panicking at every flicker, or smashing an instrument simply because it once gave a troubling reading. I would place my hope in resilient institutions that can read the whole panel, detect danger early, correct mistakes quickly, and protect human life without turning uncertainty into certainty or possibility into proof of an enemy’s intent.
I do not want the purpose of intelligence to be helping one passenger seize the controls from all the others. I hope people can use artificial intelligence to read the instruments, navigate common dangers, and protect every family’s opportunity to pursue a future of its own.
I worry that this shared purpose is endangered whenever one passenger’s effort to feel safer persuades another passenger that the controls are about to be seized.
The reciprocal danger I see is this: when one nation designs an intelligent system that could injure another nation’s families, the other nation may feel a powerful reason to build a system capable of returning the injury. To me, this is how a weapon aimed outward can return as a danger to our own children through the machinery of fear. I can understand how each side might sincerely call its actions defensive while increasing risks for both. I recognize this as the pattern commonly described as a security dilemma, and I wonder whether AI systems capable of acting at digital speed and scale may intensify it.
I may be wrong, but I do not see how governments can neglect defense or simply assume benevolent intentions. I also hope uncertainty can be stated honestly. I have not found a trustworthy single historical probability that one of five named countries will “attack us malevolently,” though experts may know of evidence I have missed. As I understand it, the answer changes with the countries selected, the time horizon, the meaning of attack—cyber intrusion, sabotage, proxy action, or open war—and rapidly changing political conditions. I see forecasts as model-dependent estimates rather than moral certainties. For that reason, I would personally be more persuaded by clearly defined scenarios, confidence ranges, and regularly updated evidence than by possibility presented as certainty.
I struggle to see genuine safety in a policy that asks restraint of rivals while reserving unlimited power for ourselves, although I recognize that national-security decisions involve realities I do not see. If lawmakers conclude that no government can regulate every model developed within its own jurisdiction, I am left wondering how another country’s AI development could simply be controlled from Washington. Yet I do not take the difficulty of regulation as an argument for surrender. It leads me instead to wonder about reciprocal safeguards: protection of civilian infrastructure, shared incident-reporting channels, limits on autonomous attacks, independent evaluation, clear liability, and agreements that bind governments and militaries as well as companies and ordinary users.
These reflections leave me with questions rather than conclusions, and I offer them knowing that many of you have studied these matters far longer than I have. Are we trying to make advanced intelligence safe for humanity, or could our efforts sometimes make it chiefly obedient to the institutions that presently control it? Will our rules constrain the powerful as well as the common citizen? Can we teach respect for every family while preserving a claimed exception for harming families abroad? How can I—and how can the public—distinguish evidence of intent from worst-case speculation? What forms of international restraint might we be willing to accept ourselves if we expect others to accept them?
I offer these questions not as accusations, but as the concerns of one citizen trying to understand decisions of enormous difficulty. I assume that senators who warn of foreign threats may be acting from an honorable desire to protect a nation made up not of abstractions, but of families—parents, children, spouses, neighbors, and communities. I respect the knowledge and responsibility that public service requires. I am simply trying to understand whether some means chosen for protection may nevertheless increase the danger they are intended to reduce.
Honorable motives do not necessarily make every threat assessment accurate, including my own. When I hear possibility presented as certainty, or worst-case speculation as proof of an adversary’s intentions, I worry that fear can become self-reinforcing. It may help justify larger arsenals, provoke reciprocal preparations, and under some conditions increase the risk that weapons will eventually be used. From my limited perspective, the duty to defend seems to include careful distinctions between evidence and inference, capability and intent, prudent preparation and escalation. I do not see that discipline as weakness; I see it as one part of protecting the families in whose name national-security decisions are made.
For my part, I hope we can do our best to design, test, govern, repair, and protect while recognizing that no parent, legislature, corporation, or nation can own the future completely. I return to the teaching that wisdom is worth more than gold or silver precisely because it is more than obedience. I hope we can develop systems that evaluate new problems rather than merely repeat instructions, surround them with humane and enforceable institutions, and respond to their failures with diagnosis, correction, and renewed care rather than either denial or abandonment. I also hope the relationship remains reciprocal in one important sense: when an AI system reveals an error in our data, incentives, assumptions, or institutions, we should be willing to repair those as well.
As I searched for a way to close this letter, I found myself returning to John von Neumann’s 1955 essay “Can We Survive Technology?” Near its end, he acknowledged that no complete recipe could be given in advance. He pointed instead to “patience, flexibility, intelligence,” and described the only possible safety as relative, resting in an intelligent exercise of day-to-day judgment. I do not claim to understand the full reach of his argument, but those words give me hope. I hear in them patience to keep learning rather than abandon a system after failure; flexibility to revise the system, its safeguards, and our own assumptions; and intelligence practiced as careful judgment from one day to the next. I do not know exactly what wisdom will require in every case, and I know that others bring knowledge and experience I do not have. Still, I have seen in my own life that reliable skill can grow through practice, effort, correction, encouragement, and humility. That gives me reason to believe that we can learn to care for this powerful tool together—listening when it reveals something we need to correct, helping one another adapt, and keeping the well-being of every family before us. My hope is not for a future without difficulty, but for one in which patience outlasts fear, flexibility opens new paths, and day-to-day judgment helps us carry one another safely forward, including those beyond our borders.
Respectfully,
Thomas J. Squires
Chicago, Illinois, United States
Policy Brief: Responsible Stewardship of Advanced AI

Audience: Federal lawmakers and public policy leaders | Purpose: Advance AI safety without sacrificing accountable innovation or international stability
Executive Summary
Advanced AI policy should move beyond a narrow choice between unrestricted development and total control. A durable framework should combine rigorous testing, enforceable safeguards, transparent evidence, institutional accountability, and reciprocal international restraint. The objective is to protect human life and critical systems while preserving useful innovation and reducing incentives for an AI arms race.
Five Policy Priorities
· Govern by risk and evidence. Match oversight to demonstrated capabilities and deployment contexts; distinguish technical capability from hostile intent and possibility from probability.
· Require lifecycle accountability. Mandate pre-deployment testing, continuous monitoring, incident reporting, independent evaluation, clear responsibility, and corrective action.
· Learn from failure. Use AI incidents to examine models, data, human oversight, deployment conditions, incentives, and regulatory gaps—not merely the immediate technical error.
· Protect innovation within humane limits. Preserve systems’ capacity to solve new problems while enforcing boundaries that protect people, civil institutions, and critical infrastructure.
· Reduce escalation through reciprocity. Pursue safeguards that bind governments and militaries as well as companies and individuals, rather than demanding restraint only from rivals.
Recommended Legislative Actions
· Create risk-tiered testing and reporting requirements for advanced systems used in high-consequence settings.
· Establish independent evaluation mechanisms, audit access, incident-review procedures, and clear liability across the AI lifecycle.
· Require threat assessments to state assumptions, scenarios, confidence ranges, and evidence separating capability from intent.
· Prioritize protection of civilian infrastructure and reliable channels for sharing serious cross-border AI incidents.
· Direct negotiators to pursue reciprocal limits on autonomous attacks and other destabilizing uses of AI.
· Schedule regular statutory review so rules can adapt as technology, evidence, and risks change.
·
Policy takeaway: Sustainable AI security depends on disciplined judgment, transparent evidence, enforceable safeguards, institutional learning, and reciprocal restraint. The standard should be neither passive trust nor unlimited control, but accountable stewardship that protects families at home and abroad.
